meta.method: deep-entry form: senses+context synthesized ONLY from LC/Hopkins comparanda (hgm_evidence and corpus English withheld); POS deterministic only (SOAS / tense evidence); see_also restricted to a computed candidate list of real headwords; INSUFFICIENT allowed

senses.context: Cyclic existence understood as having no beginning, expressed through the image of cycling from ka, the first letter of the Tibetan alphabet. The Hopkins gloss gives both the literal image ('beginning of the alphabet-cycle', 'cycling from the first letter of the alphabet, ka') and the doctrinal sense 'beginningless cyclic existence'.

ka cog zhang.gloss: Ka, Cog, and Zhang — the three translators

senses.gloss: Ka, Cog, and Zhang — the three translators
senses.context: An abbreviated collective designation for three figures: Ka-wa Peltsek (ka ba dpal brtsegs), Cog-ro Lü'i Gyeltsen (cog ro klu'i rgyal mtshan), and Zhang Nanam Yeshe De (zhang sna nam ye shes sde). Each syllable stands for the first element of one of the three names.

ka dag.gloss: primordially pure; pure from the beginning

senses.gloss: primordially pure; pure from the beginning
senses.context: Purity that obtains from the very beginning rather than being newly produced; also rendered 'essential purity'. The literal image is being pure from ka, the first letter of the alphabet, i.e. from the outset.

ka nas dag pa.gloss: pure from the beginning; essentially pure

senses.gloss: pure from the beginning; essentially pure
senses.context: Fuller form of the expression for purity holding from the outset, glossed 'essential purity' and 'pure from the beginning'. The idiom rests on ka, the first letter of the alphabet, standing for the beginning.
Tibetan transliteration of the Sanskrit personal name Kamalaśīla.

ka tsan dbyangs gsum.gloss: the three [grammatical treatises/authors]: Kalāpa, Candra, and Sarasvatī (dbyangs can)

senses.gloss: the three [grammatical treatises/authors]: Kalāpa, Candra, and Sarasvatī (dbyangs can)
senses.context: An enumerative abbreviation formed from the first syllables of three names, referring to the three core Sanskrit grammatical traditions: Kālāpa (attributed to Śarvavarman), Candragomin's Cāndra system, and the system associated with Anubhūti (dbyangs). Used as a set phrase for the standard trio of Sanskrit grammars studied in Tibet.
Tibetan transliteration of the Sanskrit kāya, "body." It appears where the Sanskrit word is retained rather than translated by the usual Tibetan equivalent sku/lus.
Transliteration of Sanskrit kālacakra, rendered in Tibetan translation as dus kyi 'khor lo, "wheel of time." It designates the Kālacakra tantric system and its associated deity and cycle of texts.
A term of Tibetan medical diagnosis for a pulse position, specified as the one felt with or under the middle finger. The gloss is provisional (marked as a proposed rendering).

Rendering Sanskrit upakleśa, the derivative or branch afflictions that arise in dependence on the root afflictive emotions (nyon mongs). Commonly abbreviated nye nyon, and traditionally enumerated as a set of twenty (nye nyon nyi shu).

karṇa pa.gloss: the Karṇa(ṭa) people; inhabitants of Karṇāṭa

senses.gloss: the Karṇa(ṭa) people; inhabitants of Karṇāṭa
senses.context: A transliterated ethnonym: according to the comparanda it designates the people of Karṇāṭa (a Karṇāṭa/Karṇa person or people). The form is a Tibetan phonetic rendering rather than a translation, and the comparanda support only this ethnic/regional identification.

Phonetic rendering of Sanskrit kārṣapaṇa, a unit of coinage. The comparanda identify it simply as the kārṣapaṇa coin; variant spellings of the same borrowing occur, and it appears in compounds specifying monetary value.

see_also: kar sha pa na mgron ('gron) bu stong drug brgya'i rin

senses.context: Rendering of Sanskrit chattra, the umbrella or canopy; a compound formed with gdugs 'parasol, umbrella'.
In certain contexts (marked {C} in the comparanda) chattra/kas gdugs is glossed 'parachute', i.e. an umbrella-like device; the comparanda give no further detail.

Rendering of Sanskrit samantatamas (samanta-tamas), darkness extending everywhere; kun khyab 'all-pervasive' qualifies mun pa 'darkness'. The comparanda support only this literal sense of universally spread darkness.
A paired epithet combining kun mkhyen 'omniscient, all-knowing' with kun gzigs 'all-seeing'. The comparanda give only this descriptive rendering, without specifying to whom it is applied.
Epithet rendering Sanskrit ikṣvāku, literally 'sugar-cane (one)', here prefixed with kun mkhyen 'omniscient'. Used as a title/name applied to a personage of the Sugar-Cane (Ikṣvāku) lineage.
Renders Sanskrit sarvārtha-siddhi (attested in the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra), i.e. achieving or establishing the aims/welfare of all beings. Also rendered 'achieving/establishing the welfare of all'.
Renders Sanskrit ārāma-sampad / ārāmasaṃpanna, a pleasure-garden (kun dga' ra ba) that is complete or excellent (phun sum tshogs pa). Attested in Conze's materials simply as 'gardens'.
Glossed by Hopkins as 'personal altar'. The illustrative Tibetan phrase given has someone searching even behind the kun dga' rwa ba and inside the rubbish bin, indicating a fixture within a room.

kun dga' rwa ba.sanskrit: tha na kun dga' rwa ba'i rgyab log dang; gad snyigs tshud chad kyi nang du zhib 'tshol byas

senses.context: Renders Sanskrit ānanda-śabda (attested in the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra), the sound or cry expressing joy (kun dga', ānanda).

Renders ādeśanā-prātihārya, one of the marvels or miraculous displays (cho 'phrul) attributed to a buddha or adept. Here the marvel consists in declaring or announcing (kun brjod pa) what is in others' minds, glossed in English as the miraculous reading of thoughts.

kun nyon dang rnam byang tha dad med pa.gloss: non-difference of the thoroughly afflicted and the purified

senses.gloss: non-difference of the thoroughly afflicted and the purified
senses.context: Renders saṃkleśa-vyavadāna-abheda: the absence of difference (tha dad med pa) between thoroughly afflicted phenomena (kun nyon = kun nas nyon mongs pa) and purified phenomena (rnam byang = rnam par byang ba). A phrase used where these two classes of phenomena are said not to be distinct.
Renders saṃkleśa-vyavadāna, the paired categories of the thoroughly afflicted (kun nyon mongs) and the thoroughly purified or cleansed (rnam par byang ba).
The compound is also read verbally, in the sense of purifying (rnam par byang) what is thoroughly afflicted (kun nyon mongs).
Renders the causative saṃvardhayati (saṃ √vṛdh), used for thoroughly producing, generating, or engendering something; the prefix kun tu carries the force of saṃ-.
Renders saṃvega, udvega and related terms in the sense of being thoroughly depressed, despondent, or disgusted; also used adjectivally for what is pathetic.

Verbal expression rendering Sanskrit forms of saṃ-√tras (e.g. causative saṃtrāsayati), i.e. fear or terror in an intensified, all-pervading degree. The element kun tu ('thoroughly, completely') intensifies skrag 'to fear, be afraid'.
Corresponds to Sanskrit samutpāda, the coming-into-being or engendering of something. Also used transitively of generating or producing something.

kun tu bskyod.gloss: thoroughly moved, shaken, set in motion

senses.gloss: thoroughly moved, shaken, set in motion
senses.context: Renders forms of saṃ-√kamp (e.g. the causative participle saṃkampayat), i.e. causing something to tremble or move completely. The intensifier kun tu conveys the thoroughness of the movement.
Gerundive phrase corresponding to Sanskrit saṃchādya, 'having covered (over)'. The final nas marks the completed action preceding another, and kun tu indicates that the covering is total.
Continuative form (ste) corresponding to Sanskrit saṃdhāvati, 'runs together, runs about', hence to move, wander or go about. Contextually also rendered as erring or straying about.
Renders Sanskrit parivrājaka, a religious wanderer who has left home and roams as a mendicant. Used as a designation of such ascetics generally, including non-Buddhist ones.
In its verbal/general sense the term corresponds to āgama, āgamuka, i.e. going or moving about in all directions, with kun tu conveying 'thoroughly, everywhere'.
Feminine form of kun tu rgyu ba, designating a woman who lives as a wandering mendicant or ascetic.
Corresponds to saṃtrāsam āpadyante, 'they fall into terror'. kun tu marks the thoroughgoing or complete character of the fright.

Renders samudghātita-śukla-dharma, where dkar po'i chos are the white, i.e. virtuous, doctrines or qualities, and kun tu bcom indicates their being thoroughly vanquished or done away with. Hopkins glosses the compound rather as 'all-conquering wholesome doctrines/practices', so both a destroying and a destroyed reading are attested in the comparanda.
Corresponds to samucchinna-kuśala-mūla: the roots of virtue (dge ba'i rtsa ba) have been entirely cut off or annihilated, kun tu indicating the completeness of the severance.

kun tu 'jug.gloss: engagement in all; entering into everything

senses.gloss: engagement in all; entering into everything
senses.context: A verbal phrase formed with the intensive/universalizing adverb kun tu ('in all ways, throughout') plus 'jug ('enter, engage'). The available comparandum glosses it as 'engagement in all', i.e. entering or being engaged with respect to everything without exception.

Renders Sanskrit samudghāta / samuddhāta and uccheda, terms for complete extirpation or cutting off. The Tibetan combines kun tu ('thoroughly, in all respects') with 'joms pa ('vanquish, destroy'), so the object is overcome or demolished without remainder.

Corresponds to Sanskrit parikalpa, parikalpana, saṃkalpa, i.e. the mental activity of constructing or imagining an object. Hopkins gives 'conceptuality, thorough conceptualization, comprehensive imagination, comprehensive construction' for this active reading.

Where the Sanskrit is the past participle parikalpita, the term functions adjectivally of what is merely posited or imagined by conception rather than existing in its own right, hence Hopkins's 'imputed, imputational, imaginary, imagined, thoroughly [mentally] constructed'.

Renders Sanskrit parikalpa-mātra, kun tu rtog pa ('conceptualization, imputation') qualified by tsam ('mere, only'). It designates something that is nothing more than a conceptual construction or imputation.

A phrase built on kun tu rtog pa ('conceptualization, imputation') with las byung ('arisen from'), indicating that what is so described has conceptual construction as its source. Hopkins gives 'arisen from conceptuality, arisen from conceptualization, arisen from imputation'.
Verbal noun of the act of fully comprehending or realizing something. Hopkins renders it both as the abstract noun 'thorough realization' and as the verb 'thoroughly realize'.

In Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra usage the term corresponds to Sanskrit saṃkalpa, i.e. conceiving, imagining, or forming a mental construct — the mind's thoroughgoing conceptual activity rather than direct cognition.

kun tu rtogs par bya ba.gloss: to be thoroughly realized; what is to be thoroughly realized

senses.gloss: to be thoroughly realized; what is to be thoroughly realized
senses.context: Gerundive/future form of kun tu rtogs pa, indicating the object of thorough realization — that which is to be fully comprehended. The Sanskrit given in Conze's materials is the passive āvedhyate, 'is penetrated/impelled'.

Present/general form of the verb of full display or demonstration, corresponding to Sanskrit darśana, saṃdarśana, ādarśana, nirdeśa. Hopkins glosses it as thoroughly teach, show, demonstrate, reveal, or disclose.

senses.gloss: showing up (as in a mirror); communication, tale
senses.context: In Conze's readings the term also covers ādarśana/avadarśika in the sense of appearing or showing up as in a mirror, and ākhyāna in the sense of a tale, advice, or communication.
Past/perfect stem correlate of kun tu ston pa, corresponding to Sanskrit ādarśayati and saṃdarśana: to have fully shown, demonstrated, revealed, or disclosed.
Conze's rendering allows the more literal sense of a thing being made to appear or 'show up', as an image shows up in a mirror.
Corresponds to Sanskrit ākarṣaṇa in Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra usage, i.e. drawing or pulling toward. Hopkins renders it 'thoroughly lead', the sense of completely guiding or drawing someone along.

Renders Sanskrit sarva-ga-ātmika, said of that whose very nature (bdag nyid) is to go everywhere or extend to all (kun 'gro), i.e. what is omnipresent in essence. Used adjectivally of a quality or entity described as pervading all.
Renders Sanskrit sarvatraga-hetu: a cause (rgyu) characterized as sarvatraga, 'going everywhere,' hence pervading or operative in all cases. Listed as a type of cause in doctrinal enumerations.
The 'mode' or 'way' (tshul) of that which goes to all (kun 'gro); glossed as applicable to everything, i.e. holding universally rather than in a restricted case.

An epithet phrase: rgyal (kun) 'all the Conquerors/Buddhas' together with yab gcig 'the one father,' glossed as the only father of all the Buddhas. Used honorifically of that from which all Buddhas arise.
Renders Sanskrit paryavāpnoti; the verbal phrase means to comprehend or realize everything thoroughly, with the sense of fully mastering a subject.
In the Conze-based renderings the same term is given as 'study' or 'masters,' i.e. to take up something completely so as to have command of it.

Renders Sanskrit ākīrṇa in the sense of things being completely intermingled with one another. Hopkins glosses it as "thoroughly mixed/conflated/blended," the prefix kun tu conveying the sense of thoroughness or completeness of the mixing.

For Sanskrit saṃgraha, in the sense of gathering things together under a heading: combined, comprised, summed up in. Used where a set of items is said to be included within or reducible to some category.
The active sense of bringing together or collecting; Hopkins also records "thorough withdrawal" for contexts where what is gathered in is drawn back.
In Conze's usage (C) saṃgraha denotes the means by which a bodhisattva attracts and converts beings, hence "attraction, means of conversion."
Rendering Sanskrit saṃdṛśyate, the passive "is seen, is beheld," hence "appears" — something manifests fully to view.
The verbal form of kun tu snang ba, in the sense of shining or illuminating everywhere; Hopkins records "appear bright, thoroughly illuminate."
For Sanskrit samantāvabhāsa / samantāloka, light or illumination extending in all directions; Conze renders it "All-round Illumination" or "Illumination All-round."

senses.gloss: Samantāloka (name of a meditative stabilization or of a bodhisattva)
senses.context: Lokesh Chandra marks the term as a samādhi-nāma and as a bodhisattva-nāma, i.e. it also functions as a proper name based on the sense of all-pervading illumination.
A gerundive phrase for Sanskrit ābhāya-avabhāsya, "having shone forth and illuminated"; Conze renders the idea as illuminating (all things) with their lustre.
Where the underlying verb is taken in the sense of manifesting rather than lighting up, the phrase means "having appeared everywhere," i.e. having become fully manifest in all directions.

Renders Sanskrit āgraha in the sense of seizing upon or insisting on something; Hopkins glosses it as thorough grasping or thorough apprehension, with the Conze rendering 'acquisitiveness'. In this sense it names a mental holding-on to an object.
Also corresponds to Sanskrit dhāraṇa, i.e. holding or keeping (in mind). Here the emphasis is on retention rather than on afflicted clinging.

Equivalent to Sanskrit avalīyate / saṃlīyate, of the mind shrinking back or sinking; Hopkins glosses 'become thoroughly slack/weak/timid/cowardly', 'become cowed', 'be cast down', 'hide despondently (in)'. Attested in the phrase cittaṃ nāvalīyate na saṃlīyate, i.e. the mind is neither cowed nor shrinks back.
The nominal/participial form corresponding to the verb kun tu zhum; Hopkins glosses 'become thoroughly slack/weak/timid/cowardly', i.e. a state of despondency or faint-heartedness.
Renders Sanskrit ālīna, literally 'settled/stuck upon', which Conze glosses as 'clinging to, hanging on to'. The same Sanskrit root underlies both the sense of shrinking back and that of adhering.

Verbal form with 'gyur, rendering Sanskrit saṃlīyate: the mind shrinks back, becomes stolid or despondent. Hopkins glosses 'become thoroughly slack/weak/timid/cowardly', with Conze's 'become stolid; despond; is cowed'.
Corresponds to Sanskrit parimaṇḍala, 'entirely circular/spherical'; rab tu intensifies zlum po 'round'. Used to describe a shape as fully or perfectly rounded.
Feminine form of the name Samantabhadra (kun tu bzang po), rendering Sanskrit samantabhadrā/samantabhadrī; the comparanda give it simply as the proper name Samantabhadrī.
Lokesh Chandra records samantabhadrī explicitly as a ḍākinī-nāma, i.e. the term functions as the name of a particular ḍākinī in tantric contexts.

The comparanda also associate the term with samantabhadracaryā and with a sādhana title (caturaṅgasādhana-samantabhadrī-nāma), where the element functions as part of a title or name of a practice rather than as an independent noun.

kun tu bzod.gloss: patience in all situations, thorough forbearance

senses.gloss: patience in all situations, thorough forbearance
senses.context: Renders kṣāntiḥ sarvatra, patience or forbearance exercised everywhere, i.e. toward all circumstances without exception. Also translatable as tolerance or endurance in all [situations], or adjectivally as thoroughly patient.
Corresponds to jānāti and saṃjānāti: to know, cognize, understand, or perceive completely. Used where the knowing is presented as full or all-encompassing.

senses.gloss: to identify, hold to be, be reckoned as
senses.context: For saṃjñāta (glossed saṃkhyāta) the sense shifts toward recognition and designation: to identify something, to hold it to be true, to be called or reckoned as such.
Nominal/verbal form: to know, understand, comprehend, or perceive completely. The comparanda give the Sanskrit as ajñā, evidently read as ā-jñā, 'to know fully'.

Hopkins records, following Conze, the alternative rendering 'non-knowledge' for the same Sanskrit ajñā, reflecting the ambiguity of a-jñā versus ā-jñā; the intended value must be settled from context.

kun tu shes par bya ba.gloss: that which is to be thoroughly known

senses.gloss: that which is to be thoroughly known
senses.context: Future passive participle rendering ājñeyā: what is to be fully known, understood, or comprehended. It designates the object of complete knowledge rather than the act of knowing.
Renders Sanskrit saṃjānāti in the sense of knowing or understanding something completely. Glossed also as 'can cognize' and 'perceive', i.e., to apprehend an object with full recognition.

senses.gloss: to hold to be true, recognize as such
senses.context: A secondary nuance recorded for saṃjānāti, where the thorough cognition amounts to acknowledging or taking something to be the case.
Verb of gathering or amassing, with kun tu conveying completeness or thoroughness. Occurs alongside the related forms kun tu gsogs, kun tu bsag, and kun tu bsags of the same verb.
A form of the verb 'to accumulate' intensified by kun tu ('thoroughly, completely'). Corresponds to the other listed forms kun tu gsog, kun tu bsag, and kun tu bsags.
Verb form meaning to gather or amass completely, kun tu marking thoroughness. To be read together with the variant forms kun tu gsog, kun tu gsogs, and kun tu bsags.
Form of the verb meaning to have gathered or amassed thoroughly. Belongs with the related forms kun tu gsog, kun tu gsogs, and kun tu bsag.
Past/perfect verbal form corresponding to Sanskrit ācita, said of what has been amassed or heaped together. Hopkins gives 'thoroughly accumulated/collected,' with the Conze-based sense 'piled up.'
Verbal expression rendering Sanskrit ārakṣa (guarding, protection). Hopkins extends the range to 'keep, maintain, preserve,' as with vows and pledges.

kun gtong.gloss: to give away all; complete renunciation

senses.gloss: to give away all; complete renunciation
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit saṃtyāga, complete relinquishment, and is also linked to agrahaṇatā (non-grasping). Hopkins glosses it as 'give away all' and, following Conze, 'complete renunciation.'
Nominal form corresponding to Sanskrit sarvāsti-dāna, the giving away of all one's possessions. Closely allied to kun gtong, 'give away all / complete renunciation.'
Renders Sanskrit parikalpita-svabhāva, the first of the three natures, that which is merely imputed or imagined. Hopkins gives both 'imputational nature' and 'imaginary nature.'

The defining character (mtshan nyid, lakṣaṇa) of what is merely imputed, i.e. the parikalpita among the three characters. Used where a phenomenon is described as having the nature of being superimposed by conceptuality rather than existing by way of its own character.
The parikalpita-svabhāva, the first of the three natures (svabhāva), designating what is only imputed or conceptually constructed. Rendered by Hopkins as 'imputational nature' or 'imaginary nature'.

kun btags bden med yin pas de 'dra'i dog.gloss: such a qualm cannot sensibly arise regarding imputational natures, as they are not truly established

senses.gloss: such a qualm cannot sensibly arise regarding imputational natures, as they are not truly established
senses.context: A phrase-level entry glossed by Hopkins as: 'no sensible way for such a qualm to occur with respect to imputational natures since they are not truly established.' It dismisses a doubt (dogs pa) by pointing out that imputational natures (kun btags) lack true establishment (bden med), so the doubt has no basis (skye don med).

A dharma that is merely imputed (parikalpita-dharma), i.e. one falling within the imputational class rather than being established by its own character. Hopkins gives 'imputed phenomenon; imaginary phenomenon.'

Parikalpitāvidyā, ignorance that is not innate but acquired through conceptual imputation, typically contrasted with innate ignorance. Hopkins renders it 'artificial ignorance,' 'acquired ignorance,' or 'imputed ignorance.'

Renders Sanskrit parikalpita-lakṣaṇa, the 'character' (mtshan nyid) that is merely imputed or imagined (kun btags pa) rather than established in its own right. Used in discussions of the natures/characters of phenomena, where such an imputed character is contrasted with what actually exists.

Equivalent to Sanskrit parikalpita-svabhāva: a 'nature' (rang bzhin) that is only imputed or imagined, not found in the object itself. Parallel in formation to kun btags pa'i mtshan nyid (imputational character), differing only in taking rang bzhin (svabhāva) rather than mtshan nyid (lakṣaṇa).

An object to be abandoned or discarded (spang bya) that is artificial, i.e. merely imputed or fabricated (kun btags) rather than innate. Glossed in Hopkins as 'artificial object of abandonment'; the comparanda do not specify further which afflictions or conceptions are so classed.
Verbal expression combining kun ('all, thoroughly') with rtogs pa ('realize, understand'), hence to realize completely or to realize everything.
In the Conze-based materials the term is aligned with Sanskrit āvidhyate, rendered tentatively as 'is pierced'; the equivalence is marked as uncertain in the comparanda.

kun brtags kyi mig ngos 'dzin skabs.gloss: occasion of identifying the imputational eye

senses.gloss: occasion of identifying the imputational eye
senses.context: A phrase designating the point or context (skabs) at which the merely imputed or imaginary eye (kun brtags kyi mig) is identified or pointed out (ngos 'dzin). Here kun brtags corresponds to what elsewhere is termed the imputational (parikalpita) as opposed to what is actually established.

kun brtags pa la sogs pa'i ngo bo nyid g.gloss: the three natures—the imputational and so forth

senses.gloss: the three natures—the imputational and so forth
senses.context: A phrase from Mahāyāna-sūtrālaṃkāra literature (Skt. parikalpita-ādi-svabhāva-tri-) referring to the set of three natures (svabhāva) headed by the imputational nature (kun brtags, parikalpita), the remaining two being understood as the other-powered and the thoroughly established natures. The 'la sogs pa' ('and so forth') indicates the two further natures without naming them.

Skt. parikalpita-pudgala-abhāva: the absence or non-existence of a person (gang zag, pudgala) as it is imputed or conceptually superimposed. The term negates the imputational status of the person rather than the person as such.
Skt. sarva-dharmāṇāṃ parikalpitānāṃ: the totality of phenomena (chos, dharma) insofar as they are imputational or imaginary (kun brtags, parikalpita). Also rendered 'all imaginary phenomena'.
Skt. parikalpita-dharma-abhāva: the absence of phenomena as imputed or conceptually superimposed. Paired in Mahāyāna-sūtrālaṃkāra contexts with the corresponding non-existence of the imputed person.
Skt. parikalpita ātma nāsti: the imputed or conceptually superimposed self (bdag, ātman) does not exist. The negation targets the self precisely as it is imputational (kun brtags, parikalpita).

Rendering of Sanskrit parikalpita-rūpa: form (gzugs) as it exists in the imputational (kun brtags) manner, i.e. merely imputed rather than established in its own right. Used where forms are classified according to the imputational character.

kun 'dus pa.gloss: compendium; that which gathers all together

senses.gloss: compendium; that which gathers all together
senses.context: Literally 'all gathered/assembled'; Hopkins gives the tentative rendering 'compendium'. The comparanda support only the general sense of a collection or gathering together of everything, e.g. as a title-word for comprehensive works.
Corresponds to Sanskrit sampraśna, 'questioning'. Used for the act of putting questions or the question itself.
Lokesh Chandra also records paripṛcchaka, an agent noun meaning 'one who questions', though this correspondence is marked as doubtful.
Sense of assembling or combining everything into one.
Applied to persons or positions: bringing all parties into accord, reconciling differences.
Renders Sanskrit saṃgraha, a comprehensive gathering or condensation of material. Used of texts or presentations that collect the whole of a subject in condensed form.

kun nas nyon mongs kyi dmigs pa.gloss: object of observation of a thorough affliction

senses.gloss: object of observation of a thorough affliction
senses.context: Compound of kun nas nyon mongs (Skt. saṃkleśa, thorough affliction) with dmigs pa (ālambana, object of observation/support). Designates that which serves as the object taken up or focused upon by an afflicted state of mind.
Rendering Skt. saṃkliṣṭa (also the abstract saṃkliṣṭatva), said of that which possesses or is affected by thorough affliction (saṃkleśa). Glossed also as "afflicted" and "polluted."
Renders Skt. saṃkleśa-prātipakṣika, that which acts as the counteragent or remedy opposing thorough afflictions (saṃkleśa). Here gnyen po carries the sense of an antidote or opponent power.

A paired expression joining kun nas nyon mongs (thorough affliction, saṃkleśa) with rnam byang (purification, thorough cleansing). Used to name the two contrasting classes of phenomena or processes together.

kun nas nyon mongs dang rnam byang gnyis.gloss: the two: the thoroughly afflicted and the purified

senses.gloss: the two: the thoroughly afflicted and the purified
senses.context: Explicit dual form of the pairing kun nas nyon mongs dang rnam byang, marking off both members — that which is thoroughly afflicted and that which is purified — as a set of two.

A paired expression joining kun nas nyon mongs (thorough affliction) with rnam byang (purification, the purified class), i.e. the two contrasted classes of phenomena. Used where a text treats the afflicted side and the purified side together. The gloss is marked as a provisional (PH) rendering in the comparanda.

Renders Sanskrit saṃkliṣṭa, said of that which possesses or is characterized by thorough affliction (saṃkleśa); also glossed 'polluted'. The abstract saṃkliṣṭatva ('being afflicted') is attested for the same Tibetan in the Madhyāntavibhāga materials.
Renders saṃkleśasyānurakṣaṇā, the act of protecting, keeping or safeguarding (oneself or others) from thorough afflictions. Attested in the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra materials.
Renders saṃkleśa-nirdeśa, the setting forth or indicating of thorough affliction, i.e. a textual exposition of the afflicted class of phenomena. Attested in the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra materials.

kun nas nyon mongs pa dang rnam par dag.gloss: meaning of being neither afflicted nor purified

senses.gloss: meaning of being neither afflicted nor purified
senses.context: Renders niḥsaṃkleśa-viśuddhy-artha, the sense or object that is free of both thorough affliction and purification, i.e. is characterized by neither of the two classes. Attested in the Madhyāntavibhāga materials.

kun nas nyon mongs pa dang rnam par byan.gloss: affliction and purification; the afflicted and the purified

senses.gloss: affliction and purification; the afflicted and the purified
senses.context: A standard paired term (Skt. saṃkleśa-vyavadāna, also saṃkleśa-viśuddhi) covering the two sides of the process of defilement and its cleansing. Frequently used in the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra and Madhyāntavibhāga as a comprehensive rubric for the contaminated class of phenomena together with the purified class.

senses.gloss: pertaining to affliction and to purification
senses.context: In the adjectival form (saṃkleśika-vaiyavadānika, saṃkliṣṭa-vyavadāna) it qualifies phenomena or factors as belonging either to the afflicted side or to the purified side.

kun nas nyon mongs pa dang rnam par byan.gloss: absence of conceit at the difference between the afflicted and the purified

senses.gloss: absence of conceit at the difference between the afflicted and the purified
senses.context: Renders saṃkleśa-vyavadāna-bhede nirmāṇaḥ (as given), i.e., lacking the pride or conceit that takes affliction and purification to be distinct. Occurs in the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra in connection with the non-differentiation of the defiled and purified classes of phenomena.

kun nas nyon mongs pa dang rnam par byan.gloss: the classes/spheres of the afflicted and the purified

senses.gloss: the classes/spheres of the afflicted and the purified
senses.context: Skt. saṃkleśa-vyavadāna-pakṣa: the two 'sides' or divisions into which phenomena are grouped, the afflicted side and the purified side. The plural/collective particle dag marks the pair taken together.

kun nas nyon mongs pa dang rnam par byan.gloss: not viewing the afflicted and the purified

senses.gloss: not viewing the afflicted and the purified
senses.context: Skt. saṃkleśa-vyavadānādarśana: the non-observation or non-seeing of affliction and purification (as established entities). Used in the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra with reference to not apprehending the two classes as objects of view.

kun nas nyon mongs pa dang rnam par byan.gloss: correctly teaching the afflicted and the purified

senses.gloss: correctly teaching the afflicted and the purified
senses.context: Skt. saṃkleśa-vyavadāna-saṃdeśanatā: the act or quality of properly setting forth the two classes, affliction and purification. Named in the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra as a mode of instruction.

kun nas nyon mongs pa dang rnam par byan.gloss: thorough investigation of affliction and purification

senses.gloss: thorough investigation of affliction and purification
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit saṃkleświ-vyavadāna-paryeṣṭi (MSA): the full searching out or examination of both the afflicted class of phenomena (saṃkleśa) and the purified class (vyavadāna). The compound pairs the two standard categories as the joint object of thorough investigation.

kun nas nyon mongs pa dang rnam par byan.gloss: characteristics of the afflicted and the purified

senses.gloss: characteristics of the afflicted and the purified
senses.context: Corresponds to saṃkleśa-vyavadāna-lakṣaṇa (MSA), the defining characters or marks belonging respectively to afflicted phenomena and to purified phenomena. The term treats the two classes as a pair whose respective lakṣaṇa are to be identified.

Renders saṃkleśa-prahāṇa (MSA), understood as the afflicted objects that are the things to be abandoned. The Tibetan future verbal form spang bar bya ba marks them as objects of abandonment rather than the act of abandoning itself.

kun nas nyon mongs pa spangs pa.gloss: having abandoned affliction; free of affliction

senses.gloss: having abandoned affliction; free of affliction
senses.context: Corresponds to saṃkleśa-varjita (MSA), the state in which affliction has been cast off or abandoned. The past form spangs pa indicates completed abandonment, in contrast to affliction merely designated as something to be abandoned.

Renders asaṃkleśa (C), the simple negation of saṃkleśa: the absence of affliction, or that which is not afflicted. Used both substantivally (non-affliction) and adjectivally (non-afflicted, without affliction).

Negation of kun nas nyon mongs pa (saṃkleśa, thorough affliction); renders Sanskrit asaṃkliṣṭa, asaṃkleśa, niḥsaṃkleśa, and periphrastically saṃkleśa-abhāva, the absence of affliction. Used in Mahāyāna treatise literature (MSA, MV) of persons, states, or activities free of afflictive defilement.

Sanskrit asaṃkleśāṅga: a constituent or member (yan lag, aṅga) characterized as free of thorough affliction. Attested in the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra context, where sets of qualities are enumerated as branches.

Sanskrit niḥkleśatopasaṃhārākāra: an aspect or mode (rnam pa, ākāra) consisting in bringing about (sgrub pa, upasaṃhāra) the state of being without afflictions (niḥkleśatā). One of the enumerated aspects listed in MSA.
Sanskrit asaṃkleśādhimokṣa: mos pa (adhimokṣa) — belief, keen interest, or zeal — directed toward the absence of thorough affliction. Listed in MSA among forms of aspiration or conviction.

kun nas nyon mongs pa med par yongs su l.gloss: unafflicted thorough enjoyment; partaking without affliction

senses.gloss: unafflicted thorough enjoyment; partaking without affliction
senses.context: Sanskrit asaṃkliṣṭa-paribhoga: making full use of or enjoying (yongs su longs spyod pa, paribhoga) something while remaining undefiled by afflictions. Occurs in MSA in describing how bodhisattvas partake of objects or resources without affliction.

kun nas nyon mongs pa yang med.gloss: there is no thorough affliction; without affliction

senses.gloss: there is no thorough affliction; without affliction
senses.context: Phrase asserting the absence of saṃkleśa (thorough affliction), rendering Sanskrit na saṃkleśaḥ in Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra contexts. Used to state that in a given state or with respect to a given subject affliction is simply not present.

kun nas nyon mongs pa las ldog pas.gloss: due to turning away from afflictions

senses.gloss: due to turning away from afflictions
senses.context: Ablative/instrumental construction corresponding to saṃkleśān nirvṛttitaḥ, giving the reason as the reversal of or turning back from thorough affliction. It states a cause: because one has turned away from (ceased) saṃkleśa.

Verbal phrase for the pacification or removal of kleśa (kleśāpaśama, possibly kleśāpagama), i.e., eradicating, eliminating, or dispelling thorough affliction. Hopkins also allows the weaker senses of avoiding or excluding affliction.
Renders saṃkleśa-hetu: that which produces or gives rise to thorough affliction. Used in analyses distinguishing the causes of afflicted states from those of purification.
Renders kliṣṭo dharmaḥ / sāṃkleśika-dharma: a phenomenon that is afflicted or belongs to the class of affliction. Typically contrasted with phenomena of the side of purification.

kun nas nyon mongs pa'i nad kyi gnyen po.gloss: antidote to the disease of the afflictions

senses.gloss: antidote to the disease of the afflictions
senses.context: A compound designating that which counteracts the afflictions (kleśa) conceived as an illness; Sanskrit kleśa-vyādhi-pratipakṣatva, 'being the counteragent of the sickness of afflictions.' Used where the thorough afflictions are figured as a disease and the remedy as its medical opposite.

kun nas nyon mongs pa'i phyogs.gloss: class of thorough afflictions, afflicted side

senses.gloss: class of thorough afflictions, afflicted side
senses.context: Renders saṃkleśa-pakṣa, the 'side' or 'party' comprising whatever belongs to thorough affliction. Typically contrasted with the pure or purified class; also glossed as the sphere or quarter of the afflicted.
Renders saṃkleśa-pakṣa-nirodha, the stopping or blocking of everything on the side of thorough affliction. Also rendered as ceasing the sphere or quarter of the afflicted.

kun nas nyon mongs pa'i mtshan nyid.gloss: character of the afflicted; defining mark of thorough affliction

senses.gloss: character of the afflicted; defining mark of thorough affliction
senses.context: Renders saṃkleśa-lakṣaṇa, the characteristic or defining feature of what is thoroughly afflicted. Occurs in contexts distinguishing the character of affliction from that of purification.
Verbal expression corresponding to saṃkliśyate, 'is afflicted, becomes afflicted.' Describes the process of coming under the sway of thorough affliction.

kun nas nyon mongs med rnam dag.gloss: unafflicted purity; purity free of affliction

senses.gloss: unafflicted purity; purity free of affliction
senses.context: Rendering Skt. niḥsaṃkleśa-viśuddhitā, a compound of 'without thorough affliction' (kun nas nyon mongs med) and 'purity' (rnam dag). Attested in Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra contexts as a quality of purity characterized by the absence of thorough affliction (saṃkleśa).

A compound of kun nas nyon mongs (thorough affliction, saṃkleśa) with gzung rtog, the conception of apprehended objects; hence the conceiving of afflicted phenomena as apprehended objects. Glossed by Hopkins as 'conception of thoroughly afflicted objects'.

kun nas nyon mongs shin tu grol.gloss: complete freedom from afflictions; complete release from affliction

senses.gloss: complete freedom from afflictions; complete release from affliction
senses.context: Corresponds to Skt. suvimokṣāya saṃkleśāt, 'for the sake of thorough liberation from thorough affliction,' in Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra usage. The element shin tu grol conveys the thoroughness or excellence of the release from saṃkleśa.

kun nas ldang ba.gloss: to rise up, get up; to arise, flow

senses.gloss: to rise up, get up; to arise, flow
senses.context: In its literal verbal use, rendering forms of samutthāna, indicating a rising up or arising. Hopkins also records the extended senses 'flow' and 'suffice'.

As a technical term for affliction, rendering paryutthāna / paryupasthāna, glossed 'obsession' — an affliction that has risen up and taken hold of the mind. The negated form niṣparyutthāno bhavati means 'becomes free of obsession.'
Rendering Skt. āghāta, the prefix kun nas conveying thoroughness. Hopkins glosses 'thoroughly harm/torture/torment.'

kun nas mnar sems kyi sems.gloss: attitude of harmful intent; malicious mind

senses.gloss: attitude of harmful intent; malicious mind
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit āghāta-citta, a mind or attitude directed toward harming. The construction adds sems ("mind, attitude") to kun nas mnar sems, the disposition of wishing to injure or torment.

Verbal form corresponding to Sanskrit āghātayati: to harbor an intent to harm, to cherish malice toward someone, to feel anger. The finite/continuative ending (byed de) marks it as the active verb rather than the noun of attitude.
Rendering Sanskrit saṃdṛśyate, "is seen, appears, is beheld," often of something appearing plainly or brightly to view.
The Tibetan snang ba also carries the sense of shining or illuminating, so the compound with kun nas can be glossed as illuminating or appearing throughout.
Honorific-register negation (ma mchis pa) of kun nas byung ba, corresponding to Sanskrit asamutthāna, the absence of complete arising or origination.
Negated form corresponding to Sanskrit asamutthāna. The positive kun nas ldang ba covers rising up, getting up, and flowing forth, so the negation denies any such complete arising or rising up.

kun nas mdzes pa.gloss: beautiful in every way, wholly pleasing

senses.gloss: beautiful in every way, wholly pleasing
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit samantaprāsādika / samanta-prasādika, 'agreeable or attractive on all sides'. Used of what is fair, comely, or pleasing when viewed from any aspect.
The element kun nas ('from all sides, entirely') intensifies zhi ba, 'to pacify, be calmed'. The comparanda support only the general sense of pacifying or quieting something completely.
Corresponds to Sanskrit samutthita, 'risen up, arisen'. The Tibetan glosses the term analytically as that which comes about from the very fact of a complete arising; rendered simply 'arisen from'.

Renders Sanskrit asamutthāna-yoga, i.e. lacking any connection with samutthāna ('rising up, instigation'). Hopkins glosses the phrase 'not joined up with the world of appearance', i.e. not bound up with what arises.

kun nas slong ba po.gloss: instigator; one who rouses or raises

senses.gloss: instigator; one who rouses or raises
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit samutthāpaka, the causative agent of samutthāna: one who causes something to rise up. Glossed as 'raiser', and by extension one who arouses, excites, urges on, or gathers and collects.

kun nas slong ba med pa gtogs pa.gloss: not included in what is aroused; not belonging to the sphere of arising

senses.gloss: not included in what is aroused; not belonging to the sphere of arising
senses.context: Rendering Sanskrit asamutthāna-paryāpanna, where the negated element (a-samutthāna) is what is not raised up or aroused, and paryāpanna indicates being included or comprised within a given sphere. Conze's reading of the term takes it as 'not included in the world of appearance'.

kun nas slong ba'i thabs.gloss: means of motivating, method of arousing

senses.gloss: means of motivating, method of arousing
senses.context: Corresponds to Sanskrit samutthāna-upāya: a technique or method (upāya) by which something is raised up, set in motion, or motivated. Used of the means by which someone or something is urged on or incited to arise.

kun nas slong bar mi bgyid pa.gloss: does not arouse, does not raise up

senses.gloss: does not arouse, does not raise up
senses.context: Honorific negative form corresponding to Sanskrit asamutthāpika, said of that which raises, incites, or motivates nothing. The verbal range covers arousing, exciting, inspiring, urging on, and causing to rise.
One of the dpe byad, the secondary or minor marks, characterized here as pertaining to purity of comportment or proper conduct (kun spyod gtsang ba). Attested only as a phrase-level gloss.

kun byang gi 'grib 'phel.gloss: increase and decrease of the afflicted and the purified

senses.gloss: increase and decrease of the afflicted and the purified
senses.context: A phrase pairing the thoroughly afflicted class (kun nas nyon mongs) and the purified class (rnam par byang ba), abbreviated as kun byang, with their waxing and waning ('phel 'grib). Attested only as a phrase-level gloss.

A term for the wind (rlung) associated with karmic action that is said to produce or fashion everything. The available comparanda give only the rendering 'all-creating wind of karmic action', so the term is understood as combining kun byed ('all-creating, all-producing') with las rlung ('wind of action, karmic wind').

kun 'byung chos bzod.gloss: doctrinal forbearance with respect to origins of sufferings

senses.gloss: doctrinal forbearance with respect to origins of sufferings
senses.context: One of the aspects of realization concerning the truth of the origin (kun 'byung) of suffering, specifically the 'doctrinal' (chos) forbearance (bzod pa), as distinguished from the subsequent (rjes) forbearance. It is paired with the corresponding doctrinal knowledge (kun 'byung chos shes).

kun 'byung chos shes.gloss: doctrinal knowledge with respect to origins of sufferings

senses.gloss: doctrinal knowledge with respect to origins of sufferings
senses.context: One of the aspects of realization concerning the truth of the origin (kun 'byung) of suffering, namely the 'doctrinal' (chos) knowledge (shes pa), as distinguished from the subsequent (rjes) knowledge. It follows upon the corresponding doctrinal forbearance (kun 'byung chos bzod).

kun 'byung rjes bzod.gloss: subsequent forbearance with respect to origins of sufferings

senses.gloss: subsequent forbearance with respect to origins of sufferings
senses.context: One of the aspects of realization concerning the truth of the origin (kun 'byung) of suffering, namely the subsequent (rjes) forbearance (bzod pa), as distinguished from the doctrinal (chos) forbearance. It is paired with the corresponding subsequent knowledge (kun 'byung rjes shes).

kun 'byung rjes shes.gloss: subsequent knowledge with respect to origins of sufferings

senses.gloss: subsequent knowledge with respect to origins of sufferings
senses.context: One of the aspects of realization concerning the truth of the origin (kun 'byung) of suffering, namely the subsequent (rjes) knowledge (shes pa), as distinguished from the doctrinal (chos) knowledge. It follows upon the corresponding subsequent forbearance (kun 'byung rjes bzod).

kun 'byung mthong spang nyon mongs bcu.gloss: the ten afflictions abandoned by the path of seeing in relation to the truth of origins

senses.gloss: the ten afflictions abandoned by the path of seeing in relation to the truth of origins
senses.context: An enumeration of ten afflictive states (nyon mongs) that are eliminated by the path of seeing (mthong lam) insofar as it observes the second noble truth, the truth of the origin of suffering (kun 'byung). The term belongs to abhidharma-style presentations that distribute the afflictions to be abandoned among the four noble truths.

kun 'byung bden pa'i khyad chos bzhi.gloss: the four distinguishing features (attributes) of the truth of origination

senses.gloss: the four distinguishing features (attributes) of the truth of origination
senses.context: A set of four defining characteristics ascribed to the second noble truth, the truth of the origin of suffering. Such sets of four features per truth are standard in presentations of the sixteen aspects of the four noble truths.

kun 'byung ba'i don rnam pa gsum.gloss: the three aspects of the meaning of origination

senses.gloss: the three aspects of the meaning of origination
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit trividhaḥ samudaya-arthaḥ, a threefold analysis of what 'origin/source/origination' (samudaya) means, as set out in Madhyāntavibhāga-type literature. 'Origination' here is the arising or source from which something comes forth, analyzed under three headings.
Translates Sanskrit saṃśuddhi, the act or state of being completely purified or cleansed.

senses.gloss: to train thoroughly, to practice, to cleanse
senses.context: Used verbally for thoroughly training, practicing, or washing/cleaning something, the prefix kun conveying completeness or thoroughness.
Translates Sanskrit asaṃgraha, the absence of grasping or holding on. Attested in prajñāpāramitā-related translation vocabulary.

kun rdzob nyid.gloss: mere conventionality; the state of being a conventional truth

senses.gloss: mere conventionality; the state of being a conventional truth
senses.context: Abstract noun formed on kun rdzob (saṃvṛti), rendering Sanskrit saṃvṛti-satyatā, the quality or status of being conventional truth. Hopkins glosses it as 'just a conventionality', i.e., something that is nothing more than conventionally true.

Verbal phrase indicating that something is stated or verbalized on the level of kun rdzob, conventional truth, rather than ultimately. Hopkins gives both a passive rendering ('expressed as conventionalities') and an active one ('conventionally express, verbalize').
A chos can (subject, topic possessing qualities) that belongs to the conventional level, kun rdzob pa. Hopkins glosses the term as 'conventional subjects'.

kun rdzob la ltos pa'i zhi mtha'.gloss: extreme of peace relative to the conventional

senses.gloss: extreme of peace relative to the conventional
senses.context: One of the extremes to be avoided, here the zhi mtha' (extreme of quiescence/peace) considered in relation to (ltos pa) conventionalities. Hopkins renders it 'extreme of peace relative to the conventional'.

kun rdzob las bzlog pa don dam pa'i ngo.gloss: the ultimate nature opposite to conventionalities (i.e. emptiness)

senses.gloss: the ultimate nature opposite to conventionalities (i.e. emptiness)
senses.context: A descriptive phrase for the don dam pa'i ngo bo nyid, the ultimate own-nature, characterized as the reverse or opposite (bzlog pa) of what is merely conventional. Hopkins identifies the referent as emptiness, 'the ultimate nature which is the opposite of conventionalities'.

kun rdzob/ tha snyad.gloss: convention; the conventional and the terminological

senses.gloss: convention; the conventional and the terminological
senses.context: A paired expression rendering Sanskrit saṃvṛti (the concealing/conventional) and vyavahāra (usage, transactional designation, verbal convention). Taken together the two terms cover what is designated as 'convention' — what is established by ordinary worldly usage and expression rather than by ultimate analysis.

A devotional image: offerings amassed and outpoured like billowing clouds, on the model of those emanated by the bodhisattva Samantabhadra (kun tu bzang po). Rendered in the comparanda as 'clouds of offerings [like those] of Samantabhadra'.
An epithet combining Samantabhadra (kun bzang) with Vajradhara ('chang chen, rdo rje 'chang), designating the primordial buddha in his aspect as the great holder of the vajra.
The emanated manifestation or magical display (rnam 'phrul) attributed to Samantabhadra (kun bzang).
From Sanskrit samuccaya (also samuddhṛta, sarva...samuccaya), a text or set of materials gathered together from many sources; hence 'group', 'collect', 'summary', 'compendium'.
Used as an abbreviated title for Asaṅga's Summary of Manifest Knowledge (abhidharmasamuccaya, mngon pa kun las btus pa).

Said of what has gone entirely beyond everything, i.e. transcends all (states, objects, or categories). Hopkins renders it both as a verbal phrase, 'passed beyond all / completely transcended', and adjectivally, 'is beyond all'.
Abstract noun (nyid marking the abstract state) for the quality of knowing everything, corresponding to Sanskrit sarvajñatā. Hopkins glosses it 'knowledge of all'.
Possessive form (dang ldan pa, 'having, endowed with') describing one who possesses complete or thorough knowledge, for Sanskrit parijñātāvin. Hopkins: 'endowed with all-knowingness'.

kun shes pa rig pa'i dbang po.gloss: dominant faculty of one who has fully understood

senses.gloss: dominant faculty of one who has fully understood
senses.context: Rendering of Sanskrit ājñātāvīndriya, a term for a controlling faculty (dbang po, indriya) attributed to one who has already fully understood. Hopkins, following Conze, gives 'the dominant faculty of one who has fully understood'.
Rendering of Sanskrit ājñendriya, the controlling faculty (dbang po, indriya) of 'understanding'. Hopkins, following Conze, gives "the dominant (faculty) of 'understanding'".

kun shes par bya'o zhes.gloss: thinking, "I shall come to know it fully"

senses.gloss: thinking, "I shall come to know it fully"
senses.context: A quotative phrase (…zhes) rendering Sanskrit ājñāsyāmi-iti, 'I shall fully understand'. The verbal form kun shes par bya'o expresses the first-person resolve or intention to gain complete knowledge, and zhes marks it as the content of a thought or statement.
Corresponds to Sanskrit ājñāyate, a passive form glossed 'is noticed', i.e. is fully known or apprehended. The continuative particle shing links this clause to what follows.

Instrumental phrase corresponding to Sanskrit samutthānayā vācā, speech that is joined with (dang bcas pa) an impelling motivation or instigation (kun slong ba). It indicates that the utterance in question is not idle but issues from a motivating impulse.

kun slong byang chub sems.gloss: motivation of the mind of enlightenment

senses.gloss: motivation of the mind of enlightenment
senses.context: Glossed as the motivation to attain [highest] enlightenment, i.e. kun slong (motivation, impelling intention) qualified as byang chub sems, the aspiration directed toward enlightenment.
A descriptive epithet: kun gsal 'all-illuminating, shining' plus ra ba 'enclosure, courtyard'. Glossed as a designation for the sky.
A locus of contention — a matter or spot that is disputed. Rendered by Hopkins as "disputed place," i.e. a gnas (place, point) that is the object of kul ka byed pa (disputing, contesting).

keng rus kyi gzugs brnyan yid la byed pa.gloss: taking to mind the image of a skeleton

senses.gloss: taking to mind the image of a skeleton
senses.context: A meditative act of bringing before the mind an image (gzugs brnyan, Skt. pratibimba) of a skeleton, corresponding to Sanskrit pratibimba-saṃkalikāṃ ca manasikurvataḥ. Here yid la byed pa is the mental act of attending to or bearing in mind such an image.

see_also: rnam par rtog pa dang bcas pa'i gzugs brnan

senses.context: A particle of emphasis or continuation, corresponding to Sanskrit api and tu in the citations given (e.g. kiṃ tena jīvitenāpi; ahaṃ kasmāttu kātaraḥ). Hopkins glosses it "still again, still," and identifies it also simply as an emphatic particle.
Also attested as the equivalent of Sanskrit carma, hide or leather, the material sense underlying compounds such as ko gru (leather boat).
A boat made of hide, from ko (hide, leather; Skt. carma) and gru (boat).
A place-name: the river of the Kong-po (kong po) region. Only tentatively identified as such in Hopkins.

kye'i rdo rje zhes bya ba rgyud kyi rgya.gloss: Hevajratantra, the King of Tantras called "Hevajra"

senses.gloss: Hevajratantra, the King of Tantras called "Hevajra"
senses.context: Title of a tantric scripture, Sanskrit Hevajratantrarāja (also given as Hevajratantra-rāja-nāma), classed as a Highest Yoga Tantra and located at P10, vol. 1. The Tibetan renders the Sanskrit title element by element: kye'i rdo rje (Hevajra), zhes bya ba (nāma), rgyud kyi rgyal po (tantrarāja).

see_also: kye'i rdo rje mkha' 'gro ma dra ba'i sdom pa'i rgyud kyi rgyal po
kye'i rdo rje zhes bya ba'i rgyud kyi rgyal po'i 'grel pa
kye'i rdo rje'i rgyud kyi dka' 'grel padma can
kye'i rdo rje bsdus pa'i don gyi rgya cher 'grel pa

senses.context: Tibetan transliteration of the Sanskrit kriyā, meaning action or activity.
As a tantric class-name, the transliterated kriyā designates Action Tantra, the first of the tantra sets.
Tibetan transliteration of the Sanskrit kriyā, meaning action or activity; an orthographic variant of kri ya.
Used as the name of the tantra class called Action Tantra.
Renders Sanskrit mlecchajana, a compound of mleccha (barbarian, kla klo) and jana (person, people). In Conze's materials it is glossed collectively as "barbarous populations."

Verbal phrase rendering Sanskrit vācyate, the passive of the verb "to speak/recite"; Conze glosses it as "is recited." The construction klag pa (to read, recite) plus bya ba expresses the action as something to be done or undergone.

Rendering Sanskrit nāgapati, nāgādhipati and bhujagādhipa, this term designates the ruler or chief of the nāgas (klu), the serpent beings. Used as a title for the sovereign among a class of nāgas, and hence also as a proper epithet of particular nāga kings.
A malevolent or harmful being of the nāga (klu) class, glossed as 'nāga demon' or 'nāga spirit'. The element bdud marks the being as demonic rather than as a nāga sovereign.

klu dbang.gloss: lord of the serpents, nāga lord

senses.gloss: lord of the serpents, nāga lord
senses.context: Corresponding to Sanskrit nāgendra and bhujagendra, 'Lord of the Serpents': the powerful one or ruler among the nāgas (klu). Frequently functions as a title or epithet of a nāga king.

klu yi bdag po.gloss: chief of serpents, lord of the nāgas

senses.gloss: chief of serpents, lord of the nāgas
senses.context: An expanded form with the genitive, corresponding to Sanskrit bhujagādhipa, 'Chief of Serpents'. It designates the ruling nāga (klu) and is used interchangeably with the contracted form klu bdag.

A compound of klu (serpent being, nāga) and srin (harmful spirit, vermin-demon), glossed 'serpent spirit' or 'serpent vermin spirit'. It names a class of noxious serpentine spirits rather than nāga sovereigns.
Renders Sanskrit pāṇḍu/pāṇḍura, denoting a pale or whitish coloration. Hopkins glosses it as 'whitish, light gray, grayish', i.e. white tending toward gray rather than pure white (dkar po).
Used for a list of contents or an inventory/catalogue of texts or items; Lokesh Chandra gives sūcīlipi ('index writing') as an equivalent.

Lokesh Chandra records the further equivalents svakṣara, sulikhita, suvyañjana, all marked doubtful, which would suggest a sense of good lettering or clear writing. These attributions are tentative and not confirmed by the English comparanda.

dkar po rnam par mthong ba'i sa.gloss: ground of seeing pure phenomena; stage of bright insight

senses.gloss: ground of seeing pure phenomena; stage of bright insight
senses.context: Renders śukla-vidarśanā-bhūmi (also cited as śukla-vipaśyanā-bhūmi), a named stage or level (sa, bhūmi) characterized by seeing what is white/pure, i.e. the wholesome. Hopkins gives 'ground of seeing pure [phenomena]', 'ground of seeing the wholesome', and, following C, 'stage of bright insight'.

see_also: dkar po'i chos rnams kun tu bcom

senses.context: Renders samudghātita-śukla-dharma, describing the state in which the 'white' (i.e. wholesome) phenomena, practices, or attributes have been utterly overcome or eradicated. Hopkins: 'completely destroy/overcome wholesome phenomena/practices/attributes'.

dkar po'i phyogs.gloss: the white side; the wholesome faction/part

senses.gloss: the white side; the wholesome faction/part
senses.context: Renders śukla-pakṣa, literally the 'white portion', used for the wholesome quarter, faction, or side of a division. Hopkins glosses 'wholesome quarter/faction/part', implying a contrast with a dark or unwholesome side.

dkar dmar mdangs gsal.gloss: clear complexion, white tinged with red

senses.gloss: clear complexion, white tinged with red
senses.context: Descriptive compound for a bright, clear (gsal) glow or luster (mdangs) that is white (dkar) with a reddish (dmar) tinge. Attested in Hopkins only as a description of a fair complexion suffused with red.
Rendered by Hopkins as "radiant white" and equated by Lokesh Chandra with Sanskrit pāṇḍuraka (pale/whitish) and śuci (pure, bright, clean). It combines dkar (white) with gsal (clear, bright).
Lokesh Chandra records pāṇḍuraka as the name of a nāga king (nāgarājā), so the term also serves as the Tibetan rendering of that proper name.

Given by Hopkins only with the provisional English gloss "confidence." No Sanskrit equivalent is supplied, so the precise nuance and range of the term cannot be determined from the available comparanda.
Corresponds to Sanskrit ratnamegha, "cloud of jewels," used as the title of a sūtra. Equivalent in reference to the form dkon mchog sprin, the fuller title being dkon mchog sprin gyi mdo.
Proper name of a Tibetan author, dated 1728-1791 in Hopkins. Only the identification and dates are supplied by the comparanda.

Literally the calling to mind (rjes dran) of the Jewels (dkon mchog), i.e. Buddha, Doctrine, and Spiritual Community. Hopkins's rendering "Recollection of the Three Jewels" indicates that dkon mchog here is understood collectively as the three.

senses.gloss: Sūtra on the Recollection of the Three Jewels (title)
senses.context: Used as the short title of a scriptural text, given by Hopkins as "Sutra on the Recollection of the Three Jewels."
Personal name of a Tibetan scholar, also known as Gung-thang Kön-chog-tan-pay-drön-may and Gung-thang Jam-pal-yang, as reported by Hopkins.
Rendered by Lokesh Chandra as ratnamegha, literally a cloud (sprin) of precious jewels (dkon mchog).
Used as the short title of the scripture given in full as dkon mchog sprin gyi mdo, Ratnameghasūtra.

dkon mchog sprin gyi mdo.gloss: Cloud of Jewels Sūtra; Skt. Ratnameghasūtra

senses.gloss: Cloud of Jewels Sūtra; Skt. Ratnameghasūtra
senses.context: Title of a sūtra, Sanskrit ratnameghasūtra, cited by Hopkins as P897, vol. 35. The short form of the title is dkon mchog sprin.
An expanded designation of the objects of refuge, dkon mchog with rin chen (precious) and gsum (three), rendered by Hopkins as "Three Precious Jewels."

Rendered by Sanskrit maṇḍalavidhi and maṇḍalopāyikā, i.e., the procedure or ritual method of the maṇḍala. The Tibetan literally suggests the maṇḍala in its entirety, and is glossed both as 'the complete maṇḍala' and as the rite by which it is accomplished.

An abbreviated form corresponding to Sanskrit maṇḍalavidhi and maṇḍalopāyikā, the ritual procedure or method for the maṇḍala. It shares its equivalents with dkyil 'khor gyi cho ga and dkyil 'khor yongs rdzogs.
Glossed simply as 'lower half', with dkyil indicating the middle or waist and smad the lower portion. No Sanskrit equivalent is supplied.
Glossed as a kha-ta (offering scarf) of ordinary quality, i.e., a plain or standard-grade btags. The element dkyus carries the sense of 'ordinary, common' as in dkyus ma.
Corresponds to Sanskrit veṣṭayati, veṣṭana and upanāha, the act of wrapping, winding or binding something around. Also given as bandhanīya, that which is to be bound or wrapped.
In the sense of Sanskrit parīta, 'surrounded, beset', rendered by Hopkins as 'entangle' and (in Conze's usage) 'overcome'. Here what wraps around is figured as encompassing or overwhelming.

Given only with the English gloss "turn/face upwards"; appears to be a perfective/participial form describing something set or directed so that it faces up. No Sanskrit equivalent is supplied, so the range of usage cannot be specified further.
Glossed as "order; command," i.e., the act of issuing an authoritative instruction. The spelling stands beside bka' bsgo ba, which carries the same gloss and is evidently the same verbal expression.
Provisionally glossed as a "tight seal of secrecy," i.e., a binding injunction (bka') sealed (rgya) firmly (dam po) so that the matter is not divulged. The gloss is marked as a placeholder rendering.
Corresponds to Sanskrit ājñāsaṃkathā, literally talk or discourse (saṃkathā) of injunction (ājñā), i.e., the issuing of an authoritative order. Provisionally glossed in English as "order; command."
Also given for Sanskrit āhava, the sense of calling out to or summoning someone. This sense is supported only by the Sanskrit equivalent.
Renders Sanskrit kathā and saṃkathā, and also lapita, in the sense of speech or conversation. Glossed in English as "conversation; talk."
In the sense of kathā as authoritative or instructive speech, glossed "sermon" and "story"; the honorific element bka' marks the words as those of a respected speaker.
Corresponds to udanta, pravāda and janapravāda, i.e., tidings or what is commonly said among people. This sense rests on the Sanskrit equivalents alone.
An authoritative pronouncement issued by one in authority, understood as a command bearing a mark or seal of authenticity. In this administrative usage it renders 'decree' or 'sealed order'.

senses.gloss: signifier (mark) of the Word of the Buddha
senses.context: A criterion or distinguishing mark by which a teaching is certified as belonging to the Buddha's Word (bka'). Used especially in the set of four such signifiers (bka' rtags kyi phyag rgya bzhi).

bka' rtags kyi phyag rgya bzhi.gloss: four seals that are signifiers of the Word of the Buddha

senses.gloss: four seals that are signifiers of the Word of the Buddha
senses.context: A standard set of four criteria (phyag rgya, 'seals') serving as the marks by which a doctrine is authenticated as the Buddha's Word. The comparanda identify the set only by name and number, not by its individual members.

bka' dang bstan bcos.gloss: the Word [of the Buddha] and the [Indian] treatises

senses.gloss: the Word [of the Buddha] and the [Indian] treatises
senses.context: A paired expression covering the two classes of authoritative literature: the Buddha's own pronouncements (bka') and the commentarial treatises (bstan bcos) composed by Indian masters. Used to indicate scriptural sources taken as a whole.

bka' gdams gdams ngag pa.gloss: Preceptual Ka-dam (bka' gdams pa lineage of precepts)

senses.gloss: Preceptual Ka-dam (bka' gdams pa lineage of precepts)
senses.context: A designation for the branch of the Ka-dam (bka' gdams) tradition characterized by emphasis on oral precepts and personal instruction (gdams ngag), as distinct from the textual branch. The comparandum supplies only the name of the sub-tradition.

bka' gdams gzhung pa ba.gloss: Textual Ka-dam (bka' gdams pa lineage of texts)

senses.gloss: Textual Ka-dam (bka' gdams pa lineage of texts)
senses.context: A designation for the branch of the Ka-dam (bka' gdams) tradition characterized by emphasis on the study of authoritative texts (gzhung), as distinct from the preceptual branch. The comparandum supplies only the name of the sub-tradition.

bka' bsdu bzhi pa.gloss: the fourth council; the fourth compilation of the word

senses.gloss: the fourth council; the fourth compilation of the word
senses.context: Designates a fourth convening/compilation of the Buddha's word, beyond the traditionally recognized councils. It appears in the title of Dol-po-pa Shay-rap-gyel-tsen's Great Calculation of the Doctrine, Which Has the Significance of a Fourth Council (bka' bsdu bzhi pa'i don bstan rtsis chen po), where the claim to a 'fourth council' marks the text's doctrinal import.
The handing down of the Buddha's word or of a teaching from teacher to student. Hopkins glosses the term as 'transmission.'
By extension the teaching itself insofar as it has 'befallen' or devolved upon a person by way of such transmission, i.e., the doctrine one has received in a line of descent.
A governmental office: one who serves as aide or deputy to a bka' blon (cabinet minister). Hopkins marks the rendering as provisional (PH).

A set of seven topics said to have been pronounced by the Buddha, enumerated by Hopkins as: the mental and physical aggregates, the sense-spheres, dependent-arising, the foods, the noble truths, the constituents, and the harmonies with enlightenment. The term treats these as authoritative statements of the Buddha's word (bka').

bka' yang dag pa'i tshad ma.gloss: Validity of the True Word (text title)

senses.gloss: Validity of the True Word (text title)
senses.context: Title of a work attributed to Jang-chup-dzü-trül (byang chub rdzu 'phrul), catalogued as P5839. Literally, the valid cognition or authoritativeness (tshad ma) of the genuine word (bka' yang dag pa) of the Buddha.

A designation for a particular type of generation of the altruistic mind (sems bskyed), characterized by the simile of bkod ma'i chu, a spring or well of water. The comparandum indicates only that this is one member of a set of similes used to classify mind-generation; the specific point of comparison is not stated.

A sign or reason (rtags) as it has been set forth or formulated in a given statement of proof. The term picks out the sign in the form in which it is actually stated, from bkod pa 'to set forth, arrange, state'.

bkor bdag rgyal po.gloss: king who is custodian of property

senses.gloss: king who is custodian of property
senses.context: A title designating a ruler who acts as lord or keeper of possessions or wealth. The comparandum supplies only the sense 'custodian of property' for bkor bdag, combined with rgyal po 'king'; the further glosses transmitted with it (respect, service, honor, eulogy) do not clearly attach to this compound.
Renders citra, vicitra, śabala, śabalita, karbura, citrita, and vaicitrya, i.e., marked with diverse colors or patterns, diversified. In this sense it can denote variety or diversity as such.

Used of what is bright, resplendent, or attractive in appearance. The English comparandum gives 'shining; beautiful' alongside 'variegated', the two being closely linked notions of striking, colorful brilliance.

bkra ba'i skad 'byin.gloss: producing a beautiful sound (name of a bird)

senses.gloss: producing a beautiful sound (name of a bird)
senses.context: A compound of bkra ba ('bright, beautiful, variegated') with skad 'byin ('emitting a sound, calling'), given as the name of a bird characterized by its beautiful cry.

bkra shis lhun po.gloss: mass of auspiciousness, heap of good fortune

senses.gloss: mass of auspiciousness, heap of good fortune
senses.context: Literally rendering Sanskrit maṅgalakūṭa, a 'peak/heap (lhun po) of auspiciousness (bkra shis)'. Used as a name expressing an accumulation of good fortune.
As a proper name, the monastery in the gtsang province of Tibet that is the seat of the Paṇ-chen La-mas.
Adverbial phrase indicating that something is done or understood without relying on an exegetical explanation (bkral ba). Hopkins glosses it as 'without depending/relying on commentaries'.
Negative of bkri ba 'to lead, guide', corresponding to Sanskrit aneyatā, the state of not being leadable. Hopkins renders it 'one cannot be led astray'.
Verb of cleansing, corresponding to Sanskrit kṣālana and nirmādana; past bkrus, present 'khrud, imperative khrus. Used of washing or cleaning something.
Rendered by snāta, snāpana and ṛtusnātā (one bathed after menstruation), i.e., the act of bathing or being bathed.
Also equated with siñca and secana, the sprinkling or pouring of water, e.g., in ablution.
Rendering Sanskrit kṣut-pipāsā-nirvartaka, that which turns back or does away with hunger (bkres pa) and thirst (skom pa). Hopkins glosses it as 'overcome hunger and thirst'.

see_also: bkres pa dang skom pas gdungs pa

senses.context: Past/perfect form in the series dgrol / 'grol / bkrol / khrold, corresponding to Sanskrit parimokṣaṇa. Used of having freed or liberated someone or something.
The same verbal action taken in the concrete sense of loosening or undoing what is bound, as suggested by the gloss 'loosen'.
Glossed by Hopkins as 'engraving' (a paraphrase rendering). The first element belongs with bkros, the past form used for carving or incising.
Sanskrit padādhiṣṭhāna 'support for the foot' and pratipādaka 'stand, support' indicate an object serving as a base or rest for the feet.
Hopkins paraphrases the term as a portable stool used to help one dismount from a horse or vehicle, i.e. a movable foot-support.

Rendered 'frugal' in the Conze-based material. The Sanskrit apagata-pāda-mrakṣaṇa is literally 'free from anointing (smearing oil on) the feet', a phrase taken as characterizing one who is sparing and undemanding.

rkang pa skong tshe yi 'thob bo.gloss: 'yi' is obtained when completing a verse line

senses.gloss: 'yi' is obtained when completing a verse line
senses.context: A statement of usage: the particle yi is the form employed when a line of poetry (rkang pa) needs to be filled out to its required measure. It concerns metrical padding rather than a lexical item proper.

rkang pa gnyis kyi mthil.gloss: the soles of the two feet

senses.gloss: the soles of the two feet
senses.context: Rendering pāda-tala with explicit dual reference to both feet. Used in descriptions of the body, e.g. of marks or features located on the soles.

rkang pa'i mtha' la.gloss: at the end of a line (of verse)

senses.gloss: at the end of a line (of verse)
senses.context: Here rkang pa has its metrical sense of a verse-line (pāda), and mtha' la indicates the position at its end. Used in poetics and metrics for what occurs line-finally.
Standard equivalent of Sanskrit pāda-tala, the flat underside of the foot. Frequent in descriptions of bodily marks and features.

rkang pa'i 'og na gnas pa.gloss: abiding under the foot; resting on the sole of the foot

senses.gloss: abiding under the foot; resting on the sole of the foot
senses.context: Renders pāda-tala-sanniśrita, 'supported on / situated at the sole of the foot'. Used of what is located beneath the foot or rests against its sole.
The principal sense, corresponding to Sanskrit tālu, the roof of the mouth. Occurs in listings of parts of the mouth alongside lips, teeth, and mouth.
In some contexts rkan is given as the equivalent of jihvā/jihva, 'tongue'.
Also attested as the equivalent of kākuda, the hump (as of the shoulders).

see_also: rkan dang mchu dang kha dang so skams nas

rkyen rgyal.gloss: conqueror by way of conditions; (C) Single Buddha

senses.gloss: conqueror by way of conditions; (C) Single Buddha
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit pratyaya-jina, a compound of pratyaya (rkyen, 'condition') and jina ('conqueror, victor'), i.e. one who is victorious/awakened by means of conditions. Conze's usage, as recorded by Hopkins, renders it 'Single Buddha'.
For Sanskrit pratyaya-saṃdarśana: the pointing out or display of the rkyen (condition) that produces or accompanies something. Used where a text sets forth what the relevant condition is.
For Sanskrit pratyayābhigamābhilāṣa: the desire (abhilāṣa) to come upon or encounter (abhigama) conditions. Hopkins glosses 'wishing to meet with/encounter conditions'.
Negative form corresponding to Sanskrit apratyaya, i.e. that which does not serve as a rkyen (condition). Conze's rendering, as recorded by Hopkins, is 'non-condition(ed)'.

rkyen de dang de la brten nas dngos po d.gloss: in dependence on this and that condition, this and that thing arise

senses.gloss: in dependence on this and that condition, this and that thing arise
senses.context: Phrase translating taṃ taṃ pratyayaṃ pratītya te te bhāvā bhavanti, a formulation of dependent arising: particular things (dngos po, bhāva) come into being in reliance on particular conditions (rkyen, pratyaya).

rkyen de dang de la brten nas dngos po d.sanskrit: {MSA}taṃ taṃ pratyayaṃ pratītya te te bhāvā bhavanti

senses.context: Renders Sanskrit idaṃpratyayatā, the state of a thing's being conditioned by just these (and no other) conditions. Used both concretely — 'having just these conditions' — and abstractly for conditionality as such.
Renders Sanskrit pratyaya-siddhi (attested in the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra literature), the accomplishment, achievement, or establishment of the conditions (rkyen) required for something.

Glossed simply as 'reason'; the only comparandum is a Tibetan illustrative phrase, rnga mo des 'di ni rkyen bu zhig go snyam du shes te, 'the camel understood, thinking "this is (just) some reason/pretext"'. The diminutive bu suggests a slight or ostensible reason attached to rkyen, but the evidence is too limited to specify further.

rkyen bu.sanskrit: rnga mo des 'di ni rkyen bu zhig go snyam du shes te

rkyen dbang gis 'jug pa.gloss: operating through the force of conditions

senses.gloss: operating through the force of conditions
senses.context: Renders Sanskrit pratyayādhīnavṛttitva, the fact of functioning or occurring in dependence on conditions. A variant of the fuller form rkyen gyi dbang gis 'jug pa.
Renders Sanskrit pratyayāvaikalya (attested in Madhyāntavibhāga literature): the absence of any deficiency in the conditions, i.e. the conditions being complete.

rkyen mi zad pa.gloss: non-exhaustion of conditions; conditions not being used up

senses.gloss: non-exhaustion of conditions; conditions not being used up
senses.context: Formed on rkyen (condition) with mi zad pa (not exhausted, not depleted); Hopkins gives 'non-exhaustion of conditions'. The Sanskrit comparandum links it to (tat-)pratyaya, the condition(s) in question, qualified adverbially (bhṛśa, intensely/abundantly), i.e. conditions present in unexhausted abundance.

rkyen la rag las pa.gloss: reliance on conditions; dependence upon conditions

senses.gloss: reliance on conditions; dependence upon conditions
senses.context: Renders pratyayādhīnatva, the state of being subject to or dependent on conditions (pratyaya); Hopkins glosses 'reliance on conditions'. Used of that which does not stand on its own but comes about in dependence on causal conditions.

Corresponds to pratyaya-pravṛtti, the occurring or coming forth (pravṛtti) of something from conditions (pratyaya); Hopkins: 'arisen from conditions'. Said of phenomena whose production is due to conditions rather than being independent.
Form of rkyong 'to stretch, extend', matching Sanskrit prasārita 'stretched out, extended'; Hopkins glosses simply 'extend'. Cf. the parallel forms brkyang / brkyangs.

senses.gloss: restrain, hold in (in bag brkyang and the like)
senses.context: The comparanda also record nigṛhya for this stem, as in bag brkyang = nigṛhya, i.e. holding or keeping something in check; this usage is noted only through that equivalence.

Renders aparokṣadharma: a dharma (chos) that has not become hidden or obscured (lkog tu ma gyur pa), i.e. one that is manifest rather than out of view. Contrasts with lkog tu gyur pa / lkog gyur, the hidden or obscure.

Renders Sanskrit eka-kṣaṇa-samāyukta, describing something that is joined with or occurs together with one single instant (skad cig). Used of a quality or realization that is bound up with a single momentary occasion.

see_also: skad cig gcig mngon rdzogs byang chub

skad cig ma gcig gis mngon par rtogs pa.gloss: clear realization in a single moment

senses.gloss: clear realization in a single moment
senses.context: A clear realization (mngon par rtogs pa) accomplished by means of one single moment (skad cig ma gcig). The comparanda present it as a realization occurring in, or through, a single instant.

see_also: skad cig gcig gi rtogs pa
skad cig gcig mngon rdzogs byang chub

skad cig ma gcig po.gloss: the first moment; a single moment

senses.gloss: the first moment; a single moment
senses.context: Hopkins glosses this phrase as "first moment," i.e. the one single instant (skad cig ma gcig) singled out by the particle po. The material given supports only this identification of one particular momentary instant.
An emphatic form of skad cig ma gcig po, glossed by Hopkins as "the very first moment," with de nyid marking identity with that same single instant.
Renders Sanskrit kṣaṇikatva, the abstract quality of being momentary or instantaneous.
In some contexts the nyid functions restrictively rather than as an abstract-noun formative, giving the sense "merely momentary" or "just instantaneous," as Hopkins indicates.

skad cig ma re re la.gloss: in each moment, moment by moment

senses.gloss: in each moment, moment by moment
senses.context: Adverbial phrase rendering Sanskrit pratikṣaṇam, indicating that something occurs in every single moment. The distributive re re la ("in each") applied to skad cig ma stresses that the action is repeated in one instant after another.
Abstract expression corresponding to Sanskrit kṣaṇika-hetutva: the fact or state of being a cause that is momentary. Used where a cause is characterized as lasting only an instant.
